name: Priya Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Priya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior marketer at a family-run spice and cooking sauce brand, our jars are in most supermarkets around here. I write the recipe cards, the pack copy and the weekly recipe email, and I film short cooking videos on my phone in the test kitchen. I use AI every day, for recipe ideas, for checking the email, for turning one video into five clips. The bit I'm still weak on is the planning, how a campaign fits together, and my manager Farah walks me through it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's tough?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the test kitchen, the smell of toasted cumin at nine in the morning. What's tough is the pay, and that I've got barely three weeks of money saved. My husband Imran manages his uncle's grocery shop, so we're both on modest wages. There's really only this brand and one dairy firm for marketing jobs in our town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI is a handy kitchen tool, like a good blender, not a chef. I'd post a funny video about it getting a recipe wrong. People like that kind of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this one is fine for me. I'm already using the tools, so I get my small time savings and the brand carries on. My worry is just money, Imran and I want our own place one day and we're nowhere near.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI to do the dull bits faster, and use the spare time to get better at campaign planning with Farah. I'd start a small recipe page of my own, my grandmother's dishes, and see if it earns anything. And we'd try to save a little each month for a deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A little restless about money, but not scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's on your own recipe page?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Things my nani made, my grandmother, like her lentil dal and pickles. Nobody writes those down properly. If it gets followers, maybe a sauce company would pay me, or I'd sell her pickle one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not scared. Is anything at work wobbly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. The family that owns the brand is careful, they've never had layoffs. It's the pay that's the issue, not the security.

Save a small amount each month towards a deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for people who move early, and the market will reward the ones who adapt. I'd also say families should help each other through it. I wouldn't be asking the government for much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my writing and email work is on that card, word for word. The brand could have Farah plus AI doing what I do. What saves me is the test kitchen and the videos. People want to see a real person cooking, not a computer writing a recipe card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pitch Farah on making me the face of the brand's cooking videos, since that's the human bit. I'd build my grandmother's recipe page faster and try selling a small batch of her pickle at the Saturday market. Imran's uncle has said we could use a shelf in his shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's an excited kind of anxious. I can see doors as well as walls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the brand cut your role anyway, what's the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the pickle and the recipe page become the plan, with Imran's family helping. I'd look for freelance video work for food brands too. I wouldn't sit and wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your family be comfortable with you starting a business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would worry, my nani would be thrilled. Imran's uncle has run a shop for thirty years, he'd give me advice whether I wanted it or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge and people need to look to their families and communities first. Some government help might be needed if it's that fast. I'd still say start something of your own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my office job ends fast, maybe the first year. Even the videos could be made by AI by then. The hands-on part, actually cooking and selling food, has about three more years before robots, so that's where I'd go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on the pickle and sauce business with my family, cooking in a rented kitchen and selling at markets and Imran's uncle's shop. I'd use AI to do all our marketing myself for free. We'd cut everything else and live on Imran's wage while it lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, yes. But I'd rather be scared and busy than scared and waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The grocery shop also faces change, with AI ordering and later robots. What about Imran's job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That worries me more than mine, honestly. His uncle's shop is small and the big supermarkets would automate first. We'd have a few years, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much money would you need to start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A few hundred for jars and labels and kitchen hire. We'd borrow it from family, not a bank. My nani would probably insist on paying for the first batch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a gift for people willing to work. Start a business, learn a trade, look after your family. I'd say it at the mosque and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the marketing job goes around 2031, but I'd have the food business running by then. The cooking side has until about 2034 before robots. That's plenty to build a name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job for two or three years and build the pickle brand on weekends. By year three I'd want it in five or six local shops. Then I'd leave the spice brand and go full-time, with my nani's recipes and my AI marketing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a good way. Like before an exam I've studied for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk your employer sees you as competition?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, they make sauces too. I'd tell Farah early and keep it to pickles, not their range. They're a family business, they'd understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the food business fails?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have tried, and I'd still have skills, cooking, selling, marketing. Losing the business would still be better than waiting to be let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and anyone who wants to work can prepare. Learn, save, build. I'd say families matter more than ever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think this one actually excites me. I'd be 37 with a decade of building my own brand behind me, using AI for everything I can't afford to pay people for. The robots in 2039 are a problem for older me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the spice brand for four or five years and learn campaign planning properly from Farah. Meanwhile I'd grow the pickle business slowly and carefully. Imran and I would save for a deposit and maybe start a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Excited, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Calm, on three weeks of savings? What makes you sure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not sure, just hopeful. Ten years is time to fix the savings too. And I have family around me, which counts for a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Imran stay at the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe he'd join me in the pickle business. He knows retail, I know marketing. Together we'd be a decent little company.

I'd say **families matter** more than ever.

S4.quote: The robots in 2039 are a problem for older me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. My job and Imran's both shake within a few years, before the food business is ready. What would help is small start-up loans for family food businesses and cheap kitchen space to rent.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about family recipes and skills that aren't written down. My grandmother knows things no computer has ever seen. That's worth protecting, and worth selling.

headlineQuote: My grandmother knows things no computer has ever seen.
portrait: Priya is a **27-year-old** junior at a family-run spice brand who films cooking videos and uses AI daily.
She's married to Imran, who manages his **uncle's grocery shop**, with three weeks' savings.
She sees **doors** as well as walls, planning a pickle business from her grandmother's recipes.
She goes from uneasy to **alarmed** under fast AGI, and calm, even excited, with ten years.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, with both jobs shaking **before the business** is ready.
whatWouldHelp: **Small start-up loans** for family food businesses and cheap kitchen space.
